title: Chapter 85 – The Wellmaster
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The summons comes by laundry bundle, tied with a red thread, and this time Zhao Yao brings it to him unopened.

He finds Jian at dawn in the dead yard behind the Pill Hall, among the snow-heaped fence posts, with a stick in one hand and a bowl of cold millet in the other. The boy from Red Ridge stands at the edge of the clearing and holds the bundle out in both palms, like an offering. His face is white. His eyes are red-rimmed.

"It came last night," he says. "The washerwoman. I burned the shirts. I did not read the slip."

"Then how do you know what it says?"

"Because I know the hand." Zhao Yao swallows. "It is the steward's. And it was tied the way my brother's last letter was tied. Twice round and a half-knot." His voice shakes. "I opened it. I read it. I am sorry."

Jian sets down the bowl.

He takes the slip. It is a leaf of thin rice paper, folded in four, and the writing is small, upright and precise.

Tomorrow, at the third watch, the Pill Hall boy is to be at the fortieth landing. You will bring him. You will walk him up in front of you, with his hands bound, as a prisoner. You will say nothing on the stair. If the stair guards ask, say he is a thief, and you are escorting him to the Hall. The Master will meet you at the top.

Do not fail. Hui is waiting.

He reads it twice. He folds it along its creases.

"Tomorrow," he says.

"Tonight, now. It was sent last night. It means tonight." Zhao Yao's mouth twists. "They have moved it up. The new moon was a month away. They changed it when the Hall found the knots."

"They are afraid."

"They are hurried." The boy meets his eyes. "It is not the same. A frightened man runs. A hurried man takes what he wants before the door closes. The Master wants you before Duan finishes the sweep."

"Yes."

"What will you do?"

The right question, thinks Jian, and a cold small thing settles in his stomach. He has known this day was coming. He has had thirty days of blindness, a flood of ink on every wall, and a pot with a pine seedling to remind him. He has not known what he would do when it came.

He knows now.

"I will go," he says.

* * *

"No," says Feng, flatly.

They are in the Medicine Valley dispensary, behind the Overseer's office, where the Healer has laid Feng on a cot with his leg in a cradle of splints and a ration of bitter tea. It is the afternoon of the thirty-first day. The room is warm and dim and smells of camphor. Wei Chen sits on a stool by the window with a book. He does not look up when Jian comes in, and he does not leave.

"You cannot ask me to agree," says Feng. "You are ten."

"I am not asking."

"You are telling me you intend to walk up the Hundred Stairs at the third watch with your hands bound, to meet a Blood Shadow Master, a Well-stage cultivator, in the dark, alone." His voice is very quiet. "I would like to hear how that is not suicide."

"Because I will not be alone." Jian sits on the end of the cot. "And because the stair is mine."

He says it plainly, and watches his brother's face change.

"The array is a pressure array," he says. "It presses on a person in proportion to his depth. A boy of the third layer feels it as a hand. A first-ranker of the ninth feels it as a weight. A Purple Mansion cultivator would feel it as..." He stops. "It is a measure. The Master has never climbed it. He will not know how it behaves with a stronger man on it. Nobody does. It has not been tried."

"You mean to try it."

"I mean to be standing where it is not pressing, while he is standing where it is."

Feng stares at him. On the stool by the window, the Inner disciple has lowered his book.

"The landing has a vent," says Jian. "A seam in the northeast post, behind the jade. The array lets out pressure through it, like a kettle through its spout. If the spout were stopped, the pressure would build in the landing itself." He lets his breath out. "It would build on whatever was heaviest."

"How do you know about the vent?"

"I have been looking at it for a month."

"With what?"

With the thing I do not name. "With a pangolin who feels seams."

The silence stretches. Wei Chen's hands are quite still on the cover of his book.

"I will not ask how you know the array's structure," he says at last, softly. "I am a Medicine Valley disciple. I do not know arrays. But I know that the Founders' stair was cut by a hand that did not believe in accidents. If there is a vent, there was a reason for it." He closes the book. "I have a duty tonight. I am to inspect the stair guard at the second watch. It is a duty I may extend. The guard is to be relieved at the third."

"Senior Brother."

"I did not say anything." The long calm face is unreadable. "I said that I have a duty, and that duties are long."

He is making a hole in the guard. Jian bows his head. He does not trust himself to speak.

"Go," says Feng, to the ceiling. His eyes are shut. "Go, and take care, and tell Zhao Yao that if he lets you die I will find him." A pause. "And I would like it noted that I think you are mad."

"Noted."

"And that I would do the same."

* * *

He sleeps for an hour in the afternoon, which is the most he can manage, and eats a bowl of millet with Bai's dried plum on the side. He goes to the herb store and talks to no one. He sits among the roots with Pebble in his lap and the panel open at the edge of his sight, and reads it, line by line.

```
CE: 50
Scan: ONLINE (first-use calibration x3 pending).
Fabrication: ONLINE.
Synthesis: ONLINE (Level 2).
Seam-sight: ONLINE (passive, range extended).
```

Fifty. It is not a great deal. It is not enough to scan the array, which would cost fifteen for the calibration alone. It is not enough to fabricate anything but a handful of pins. He sits and does the sums, and comes to the same answer every time: he cannot afford to use it.

Seam-sight is free.

He has been using it for two days. It is a strange, lovely, terrible gift: the world as a lattice of joins. A wall is a thousand small cracks, each with a direction. A tree is a lattice of rings. A man is a thing of seams, and he has taught himself to keep his eyes from resting on them. Last night, from the foot of the Hundred Stairs, he stood for an hour and looked up the whole length of the stair, and traced it from landing to landing, and found the vent.

It lies in the northeast post of the fortieth landing, a hairline fissure behind a plate of jade. It runs down through the mountain for sixty feet and out through a spring on the north face. The array breathes through it. Every time a disciple climbs, the array pushes down and the vent pushes out, and the pressure is released in a long slow sigh into the mountain.

If the vent were closed, the sigh would have nowhere to go.

Pebble.

The pangolin lifts its head. In the warm dim of the herb store its eyes are very bright.

A seam, Jian sends. A long one. Narrow. In a post. I want you to go into it and make it close.

There is a pause, a long one. Then, in his mind, a picture: the vent, drawn in thin bright lines, and a small bronze shape curled in the middle of it with its scales flared. It looks like a plug. The picture shivers, and he feels the creature's doubt.

It will not like it.

No.

It will push.

Yes. He strokes the scales. I know. I am sorry. I would not ask if there were any other way.

A warm slow wash of feeling comes up through the bond: reluctance, and pride, and a kind of grim amusement. The pangolin turns round once in his lap, and settles, with its snout against his wrist.

Good, says the feeling. I am a very good plug.

* * *

The Hundred Stairs by night is a river of white.

There is no moon, but the snow gives light enough, and a faint pale glow rises from the jade posts at every landing. Jian walks up the first flight with his wrists tied in front of him, in a loop of coarse rope, with a boy of fourteen behind him holding the end. His tunic is torn at the shoulder. There is mud on his face. He has made himself look like a boy who has been caught.

Zhao Yao does not speak. His breath comes short and hard. His hand on the rope is shaking.

At the tenth landing, two inner disciples in white stand under a lantern, with spears. Jian does not know them. They look at him, at the rope, at the Zhao boy, and one of them steps forward.

"Halt. What is this?"

"A thief," says Zhao Yao. His voice is a croak. "From the Pill Hall. He was caught with a root from the Valley. I am to take him to the Hall, by the Deacon's order."

"By the stair?"

"The Enforcement Hall is at the top."

The guards look at each other. The one with the lantern raises it. For a heartbeat, his eyes rest on Jian's face, and the boy sees him think: this is the Pill Hall one. Sees him think: this is the one who stood on the fortieth landing.

"Pass," says the second guard, quickly, and steps aside. "Do not linger."

They go on. At the twentieth landing, there is no one. At the thirtieth, a lantern burns on a post, untended. Jian's eyes follow its yellow light up the empty stair, and he realizes that Wei Chen has been as good as his word.

Thank you, he thinks.

The pressure begins at thirty. It is light for the first few steps, then heavy, then very heavy. He lets it come. He has taught himself to feel it without fighting, and the Seal under his navel is calm. The Veil holds. By the thirty-eighth landing he is a youth of twenty-one bent under a weight that a third-layer cultivator should bend under, and his breath comes in small white puffs.

The fortieth landing opens in front of him.

* * *

The new post is white. It stands at the center of the platform, taller than the old one, cut from fresh jade, with a disk of polished stone at its heart. The old paving has been relaid. The four corner posts glow faintly. The snow has been swept.

And at the far side, at the head of the next flight, where the stair climbs on into the haze, a figure is waiting.

He is very tall. He stands against the white of the cloud like a pillar of gray stone, in a long hooded robe that falls to his feet and hides everything but his hands. They are long, thin and pale, and they hang at his sides, perfectly still. The hood is pulled forward over the face. No breath rises from it into the cold.

A wall that walks.

Pebble, in the bag at Jian's belt, has gone as rigid as a stone. The thin cold line of feeling that comes up through the bond is a single word, repeated over and over: Wrong. Wrong. Wrong.

"You are late," says the figure.

The voice is deep and slow. Each word is laid down carefully, a stone on a stone. It is the voice Zhao Yao described, and it is worse, because it is not coming from the hood. It comes from the air. It comes from the stone. It comes, Jian thinks, from the whole landing, as though the platform itself had learned to speak.

"The stair guard," says Zhao Yao hoarsely.

"Was delayed." A faint, dry sound, as of a smile. "You did well, boy. You may let go of the rope."

Zhao Yao lets go. He steps back. His hands are open at his sides, and his face is the color of paper.

"Your brother is well," says the Master. "He is asleep in a warm house. I am a man of my word." The hood turns, a hair, toward Jian. "Lin Jian."

"Master."

"You know what I am?"

"A Well." The word is a whisper. "Of the Blood Shadow."

"Of the Purple Mansion, and the Well, and a number of other things, none of which you need." The pale hands lift a little. "I am told you cannot see. I am told you have lost the thing in your head. I am told you are, for the first time since you left your village, no more than what you look like: a child, with a pangolin and a rope." The voice is gentle. "I am sorry. It is not a thing I enjoy. But my order has waited six hundred years. I do not intend to wait for another sunrise."

Six hundred years.

It is the first time the Master has said it aloud. It lies in the cold air between them like a coin on a table.

"I need a hand," says the Master. "A small one. The right. Laid on that disk." He nods at the post. "It is a trifling thing. You have done it once already. It does not hurt."

"What will it do?"

"It will open." The deep voice is almost tender. "It will open what the Founder shut. And you will go on living, which is more than the last one did."

The last one. The child. The Disciple of the Fortieth Step. The boy who went in, and did not come out.

"I will," says Jian.

He says it quietly. He lifts his bound hands. Zhao Yao makes a small choked sound behind him.

"Cut the rope," says the Master.

A dark thing flickers in the air. The rope parts. Jian's hands fall free.

He walks to the post.

* * *

The disk is white and warm.

It glows faintly as he comes near, a low pale gold, and the hollow in its face waits, the small right-handed hollow, copied from the old disk by a mason who did not know what he was copying. Behind him, the Master has not moved. The air is thick with the weight of his regard. Jian can feel it on his neck, patient and enormous, like a hand on a bolt.

Seam-sight.

He lets his eyes soften. The world comes apart. Under the polished stone, the lattice spirals inward, ring on ring, to the heart of the post. The dock waits there, dormant, a seven-lobed ring of cold silver. He does not look at it. He looks to the right, to the northeast corner of the landing, where a post of white jade stands at the edge of the platform with a plate of carved stone on its inner face.

The vent is there. It is a hair of darkness, no wider than a thread.

Now.

He does not say it aloud. He sends it down the bond with all the clarity he has. The bag at his belt gives a single hard shudder, as if something inside it had made up its mind, and then the flap falls open and a small bronze shape flows out onto the stone, unrolls, and runs.

It is faster than anything he has ever seen. It crosses the paving in a streak, up the corner post, along the plate. It is gone into the seam before a man could draw breath.

The Master turns his head.

"What was..."

Jian lays his palm on the disk.

* * *

The array wakes.

It is not the low hum of the trial. It is a roar. A column of white light erupts from the post, straight up into the sky, and the whole landing blazes. The jade corner posts flare. The paving ignites in lines of gold. The mountain itself seems to take a breath, and the breath is a sound, a vast, slow, tremendous note, like a bell the size of a valley.

The key has been placed. The lock has been asked.

And the lock, for the first time in six centuries, answers by measuring the man who asked.

It does not measure Jian. It reads him in an instant: twenty-one years old, five elements, third layer by the Veil, ninth by the Seal; a child. It lets him go. It lets him go so lightly that he almost falls. The pressure that has been bending his shoulders for a hundred steps lifts off him like a cloak.

It turns instead on the other thing on the stair.

"No," says the Master.

He has taken a step. It is only a step, his first in a quarter of an hour, and it breaks the stillness of his body as a stone breaks the surface of a pond. The hood falls back. Beneath it is a long gray bald skull, a face like worn stone, eyes like drops of tar. The mouth opens.

The first weight hits him.

It is the whole array. It is every breath of the mountain, gathered in a single point, a hundred and twenty pressures laid one on another and poured into a Purple Mansion body. The landing groans. The snow around him vaporizes in a ring. His knees buckle, and he catches himself on one hand, and his head comes up, and in the black eyes there is something that Jian has never seen on the face of a Blood Shadow creature.

Fear.

"The vent," says the Master, thickly. "Where is the vent..."

He lifts a hand. A coil of black light unwinds from his fingers and lashes toward the northeast post. It strikes the jade with a crash. The plate cracks. A thread of steam shoots out and dies.

Pebble!

Holding. The thin, bright, desperate answer comes through the bond in a rush. Pushing. Pushing. Holding.

The Master staggers. The array presses on. His robe tears; his shoulders sag; the gray skin of his hands splits along the knuckles and weeps black. He turns his head, and the tar-black eyes fix on Jian with an expression of hatred so pure it is almost respect.

"You," he says. "You knew."

"I knew it was a measure." Jian's voice is hoarse. His hand is still on the disk. "I did not know what it would measure when it was asked about you."

"My order has waited six hundred years..."

"So you said."

"We have waited for this stair..."

The Master's knees hit the stone. He puts both hands flat on the paving, and the paving cracks beneath them. His spine bows. The sound that comes out of him is the dry grinding of a millstone, and it goes on and on, and Jian watches the great gray body fold, joint by joint, into the earth.

"Not the last," says the Master, from the ground.

It is hardly a voice any more.

"Not the last. There are Wells beyond Wells. You have opened a door." The head turns. The tar-black mouth stretches. "What you shut tonight, others will open. We have been waiting a very long time."

The array flares white.

When the light clears, there is a pile of fine gray dust on the paving, shaped like a kneeling man. A breath of wind comes down the stair and lifts the top of it, and the dust goes up in a long pale plume, and is gone.

* * *

```
TARGET ELIMINATED.
Classification: Blood Shadow (Well-stage), infiltrator, high-value.
Method: ancient Gate mechanism (Hundred Stairs array, vent closure).
Reward: +130 CE.
CE: 50 -> 180.
```

He reads it with his palm still on the disk.

It is very quiet. The roar of the array has died. The corner posts glow dully, and the column of light has dwindled to a faint steady shimmer around the new post. Snow is falling again. He becomes aware of a trembling in his hand, and takes it from the disk, and sees that it is bleeding where the stone bit into his palm.

Pebble.

Here. The reply is faint and cross. A small bronze shape crawls out of the northeast seam, shakes itself, and drags itself across the paving to Jian's feet, where it collapses in a heap with all its scales wilted. Pushed, it adds, with great dignity. Very hard. I would like a plum.

He picks it up. He holds it against his chest. He is laughing, he finds, a thin high breathless sound that is half sobbing, and he cannot stop.

"Lin Jian."

Zhao Yao stands on the rim of the platform where the Master left him. He has not moved. His hands are open at his sides, and his mouth is open too, and he is looking at the patch of bare stone where the dust was. His eyes are wet.

"Is it..."

"It is finished," says Jian. "For now."

"Hui..."

"Your brother is in Red Ridge. He is alive. The steward is still there." He draws a breath. "We will go for him. I will help. It is the least I owe." He looks at the boy. "You took a great risk tonight. I will not forget it."

Zhao Yao sinks to his knees. He does not weep. He sits on the stone with his hands over his face, and his shoulders shake, and the snow falls on his hair.

He has a debt to me now, thinks Jian, and I to him. We will have to settle it.

It is a thought for another day.

* * *

The Elders arrive at dawn.

He has not moved. He sits on the edge of the fortieth landing with his back against the new jade post, a small, cold, filthy boy in a torn gray tunic, with a pangolin asleep on his lap and Zhao Yao slumped beside him. The sky has gone the color of a pearl. A thin gold line is lifting along the eastern ridge. Below, the whole Court is waking: smoke from the kitchens, the clink of buckets, a distant bell.

They come up the stair in a body.

Shen Wuye leads, in white, his lean face composed and his hands folded in his sleeves. Behind him, Elder Duan tramps up the flight with a face like a thundercloud and a dozen iron guards at his back. Behind them, a stout rumpled figure in plum-stained green is breathing hard and carrying a paper twist. And last of all, in a plain gray robe, with a hand on the arm of a young Inner disciple in indigo, a tired old man with a long beard and a trembling hand.

They stop along the rim of the landing.

Nobody speaks. The wind lifts a little snow. On the paving between the posts, a ring of black scorch marks surrounds a patch of bare stone. The old stone is cracked. The jade plate on the northeast post is split from top to bottom. The air still smells of burnt hair and hot iron.

"Disciple Lin," says Shen Wuye, at last.

"Arbiter."

"You were on the stair."

"Yes, Arbiter."

"You were not on the stair last night by leave of the Hall."

"No."

"The guard was gone from the thirty-first landing, the thirty-second, the thirty-third. The array has been, I am told, rung like a gong. It was heard in the Library." The cool voice does not rise. "A column of light was seen from the Pill Hall to the Medicine Valley. And I find on my landing a scorch ring the size of a threshing floor, a broken plate, and a youth of twenty-one who is not hurt."

"I am a little hurt," says Jian.

"You are bleeding from the palm."

"It is a small cut."

Elder Duan makes a sound in his throat like a boulder shifting. He steps forward. His flat gray eyes travel over the landing: the ring, the posts, the dust in the corners. They fix on the pangolin, and the boy who holds it, and the boy beside him. They fix on the white post.

"What was here?" he says.

"A Blood Shadow," says Jian. "A Well. The one who wore the Deacon's face."

"Where is it?"

"Dead."

"Who killed it?"

He opens his mouth. He closes it. He looks at the Elders, the white one and the gray one and the plum-stained one and the tired old one in the indigo shadow, and he knows, with perfect clarity, that this is the end of the Pill Hall boy. The lie of the third layer, the lie of the slow wheel, the thin soft story that he has told in a hundred rooms and worn for three months like a cloak. It was a good cloak. It has served. It will not serve here.

What I am has gone before me, he thinks. And they have come to look.

"The stair," he says. "I asked it a question. It answered."

Shen Wuye's face does not change. But a very small thing happens at the corner of his mouth, and he lowers his eyes.

"The Elders will hear you," he says. "Now. In the Hall of Open Session. Come."

It is not a request. It is not, quite, a command. It is a door, held open, with a long corridor behind it and a great many people waiting at the other end.

Jian rises. His knees are stiff. He tucks the sleeping pangolin into the breast of his tunic and looks down at Zhao Yao, who has lifted his head and is staring at him with an expression of terror, and he says, in a low steady voice that does not shake:

"Stay here. Say nothing. I will come back."

He is not certain it is true.

He follows the white robe down the stair.
